\begin{document}

\title{When Do Variational Quantum Circuits\\ Keep Federated Training Data Private?}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{AJ Barea}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Rochester Institute of Technology\\
Rochester, NY, USA\\
ajb6289@rit.edu}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Federated learning shares gradients instead of data, and gradient matching can rebuild a client's
input from its gradient. For variational quantum circuits (VQCs) the literature disagrees on
whether that attack works. We test it on simulated data re-uploading circuits with 4 and 8 qubits,
an attacker who knows the circuit and its parameters, and exact second-order gradients of the
matching loss. Over 400 attacks, every circuit with one encoding layer and at least two trainable
layers gave up its input on 20 of 20 seeds. At a fixed parameter count, trading trainable layers for
encoding repetitions left the attack stuck in local minima more often. At 8 qubits and 120
effective parameters, the input was recovered on 20, 18, 8 and 2 of 20 seeds for 1, 2, 4 and 8
repetitions. Against 10 restarts, shot noise in the client's gradient protected 8-qubit circuits
at 100 shots per expectation value. For circuits the noiseless attack breaks, the reconstruction error then fell as
roughly $S^{-1/2}$ in the number of shots $S$. Raising the attacker's budget from 10 to 50 restarts recovered the input on 17--18 of
20 seeds for three of the four hardest 8-qubit circuits, and on 5 of 20 for the fourth. Encoding
repetitions raise the cost of the attack; of the four circuits retested at 50 restarts, only the most
repeated one still held on most seeds.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
federated learning, gradient inversion, variational quantum circuits, privacy
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
In federated learning (FL), clients train a shared model on their own data and send the server
gradients or weight updates instead of the data~\cite{mcmahan2017}. On classical neural networks
those gradients can be inverted. The server searches for an input whose gradient matches the one it
received, and it often recovers the training example~\cite{zhu2019,geiping2020}.

For VQCs used as the FL model, three papers from one group reach different conclusions. Kumar et
al.~\cite{kumar2023} argue that expressive encodings give VQCs inherent privacy, because the
gradient equations become high-degree trigonometric polynomials with exponentially many local
minima. Papadopoulos et al.~\cite{papadopoulos2025} reconstruct inputs numerically from 2- and
6-qubit VQCs that are ``sufficiently overparameterized''. Heredge et al.~\cite{heredge2025} prove
that properties which make a VQC trainable also let an attacker extract snapshots of the encoded
state. The three papers use three different definitions of overparameterization and three
different attacks, and none simulates shot or hardware noise in the attacked circuit.

This report measures where the attack works on one controlled family of circuits. The
contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
  \item A sweep of 400 gradient-matching attacks over 4- and 8-qubit re-uploading circuits that
  trades encoding repetitions against trainable layers at a fixed parameter count
  (Section~\ref{sec:rq1}).
  \item A measurement of how finite-shot gradient estimates change the attack, from $10^2$ to
  $10^6$ shots per expectation value (Section~\ref{sec:rq2}).
  \item A restart-budget experiment showing that most attacks counted as stuck succeed with more
  restarts, which turns ``stuck'' into a cost measured in restarts per success
  (Section~\ref{sec:budget}).
  \item An open-source JAX simulator and attack harness, checked against PennyLane, with every
  attack's raw result committed (\url{https://github.com/ajbarea/csci739-qfl-privacy}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Background and Related Work}
\subsection{Gradient Inversion in Federated Learning}
In the deep-leakage attack~\cite{zhu2019}, the server holds the model parameters $\theta$ and a
client's gradient $g = \nabla_\theta L(x, y;\theta)$. It minimizes
$\|\nabla_\theta L(\hat x, y; \theta) - g\|^2$ over a candidate input $\hat x$. This needs the
gradient of a gradient, which automatic differentiation provides. Geiping et
al.~\cite{geiping2020} showed the attack recovers high-resolution images from realistic networks
and that sharing averaged updates over several local steps does not prevent it.

\subsection{Variational Quantum Circuits and Data Re-uploading}
A VQC encodes a feature vector $x$ into rotation angles, applies trainable gates with parameters
$\theta$, and outputs an expectation value $f(x;\theta)$. Repeating the encoding $r$ times, with
trainable blocks in between, is data re-uploading~\cite{perezsalinas2020}. With single-qubit
Pauli-rotation encodings, $f$ is a trigonometric polynomial in each feature whose frequencies grow
with the number of repetitions~\cite{schuld2021}: $r$ repetitions give integer frequencies up to
$r$. Every gate in our circuits is a Pauli rotation, so gradients follow from the parameter-shift
rule~\cite{schuld2019}, which is how a device would compute them.

\subsection{Competing Claims for VQCs}
\emph{Inherent privacy.} Kumar et al.~\cite{kumar2023} encode each feature on $m$ qubits with
exponentially spaced frequencies (a ``Fourier tower'' map), so the gradient has frequencies up to
$(5^m-1)/2$. They count local minima of the matching loss growing as $e^{1.48m}$, and an
ADAM attacker (60 iterations from 10 random starts) does no better than guessing at $m = 3$. They
assume the worst case for the client: batch size 1, exact gradients, and a known label.

\emph{Numerical inversion.} Papadopoulos et al.~\cite{papadopoulos2025} attack 2- and 6-qubit
angle-encoded VQCs with finite-difference gradients, a moving-average low-pass filter and an
optional Kalman filter. One attack recovers the input (mean squared error $\le 0.005$) on 100\% of
2-qubit trials and 40--80\% of 6-qubit trials. They call a model overparameterized when its
parameters give at least as many gradient equations as there are unknowns.

\emph{Privacy versus trainability.} Heredge et al.~\cite{heredge2025} consider an observable that
lies in the circuit's dynamical Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. They show that once the number of
parameters is at least $\dim\mathfrak g$, a linear system recovers a snapshot of the encoded state,
which they call a weak privacy breach. Recovering $x$ itself needs further conditions on the encoding. In their analysis,
Kumar et al.'s circuits stay private only because their Lie algebra is exponentially large, which
also makes them untrainable.

Our encoding is linear re-uploading, not the Fourier tower. Its frequencies grow linearly in $r$,
so our results test the mechanism Kumar et al.\ propose (more frequencies, more local minima) on a
different encoding, not their construction.

\section{Threat Model}
The server is honest but curious. It follows the FL protocol and tries to learn the client's input
from what it sees. It knows the circuit architecture, the current parameters $\theta$ (it sent
them), the observable, the loss, and the label $y$. It observes one client's gradient for a single
training example. This matches Kumar et al.'s worst case for the client~\cite{kumar2023}. The
client's parameters are untrained, drawn uniformly from $[0, 2\pi)$.

\section{Method}
\subsection{Circuit}
On $N$ qubits, the circuit repeats the following $r$ times: encode feature $x_q$ as $R_Y(x_q)$ on
qubit $q$, then apply $\ell$ trainable blocks. Each block is $R_Y(\theta)R_Z(\theta)$ on every qubit
followed by a CNOT chain $0\to1\to\dots\to N-1$. The output is
$f(x;\theta) = \tfrac1N\sum_q\braket{Z_q}$ and the client's loss is $(f - y)^2$ with $y = 1$. A
single-qubit observable would leave some inputs outside its light cone, so they would never reach
the gradient. The mean over all qubits avoids that, and a test checks it on four circuit shapes.

The circuit has $2r\ell N$ parameters. The last block's $R_Z$ gates are followed only by CNOTs and
a $Z$-diagonal measurement, so they never change the output. We report the
$2r\ell N - N$ \emph{effective} parameters, and a test confirms on three circuit shapes that
exactly these have nonzero gradient. Inputs are drawn uniformly from $[0,\pi)^N$.

\subsection{Simulator}
The attack differentiates through a gradient, so it needs second-order automatic differentiation.
In the original feasibility spike, PennyLane~\cite{bergholm2018} with autograd took 133~s for five
attacks of 5 restarts each on a 4-qubit circuit with $r = \ell = 4$. Compiling the PennyLane
circuit with JAX unrolls every gate, so compile time grows with circuit depth. We wrote a
statevector simulator in JAX~\cite{jax2018} that scans over repetitions and blocks, so it compiles
once per circuit shape; at 8 qubits the first call took under ten seconds on a 6-core CPU. Tests pin
its output probabilities and gradients to PennyLane's \texttt{default.qubit} within $10^{-12}$.

\subsection{Attack}
The attacker minimizes
\[
  \mathcal L(\hat x) = \big\|\nabla_\theta (f(\hat x;\theta) - y)^2 - g\big\|_2^2
\]
with L-BFGS-B~\cite{byrd1995}, using the exact gradient $\nabla_{\hat x}\mathcal L$ from automatic
differentiation, for at most 500 iterations. It starts from 10 points drawn uniformly from
$[0,\pi)^N$ and keeps the restart with the lowest $\mathcal L$, which is all an attacker without
the true input can do.

\subsection{Outcomes}
Each attack ends in one of four outcomes:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Recovered}: every feature lies within 0.05~rad of the true input, measured modulo
  $2\pi$ because $R_Y(x+2\pi) = -R_Y(x)$ differs only by a global phase.
  \item \emph{Close}: not recovered, but every feature within 0.2~rad. Under shot noise this is
  the best the attacker can do, and it still reveals the input to within that angle.
  \item \emph{Ambiguous}: an input further away that matches the gradient at least as well as the
  true one, $\mathcal L(\hat x) \le \mathcal L(x) + 10^{-6}\|g\|^2$. For an exact gradient
  $\mathcal L(x) = 0$, so this is a second exact preimage.
  \item \emph{Stuck}: a local minimum that matches worse than the true input.
\end{itemize}
Under shot noise we also report the median reconstruction error. Outcomes are recomputed from each
restart's stored error and loss, so a change of threshold needs no rerun. Every setting uses 20 seeds, each
with its own input and parameters. Error bars in Fig.~\ref{fig:map} are 95\% Wilson intervals.

\subsection{Shot Noise}
For RQ2 the client estimates its gradient as a device would. Each $\partial f/\partial\theta_j$
comes from the parameter-shift rule, and each of the $2P+1$ expectation values (including $f$
itself) is the mean of $S$ sampled measurements. The attacker still matches with its noiseless
model.

\section{Experiments and Results}
\subsection{RQ1: Encoding Repetitions Versus Trainable Layers}\label{sec:rq1}
We ran every $(r,\ell)$ with $r\ell\in\{1,2,4,8\}$ at 4 and 8 qubits: 20 circuit shapes and 400
attacks. Table~\ref{tab:rq1} gives the outcome counts and Fig.~\ref{fig:map} plots the recovered
fraction at a fixed parameter count.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/privacy-map.pdf}
\caption{Fraction of 20 seeds recovered against encoding repetitions $r$, with $\ell = $
product$/r$ trainable layers, so each line holds the effective parameter count fixed. Bars are 95\%
Wilson intervals.}
\label{fig:map}
\end{figure}

Three regimes appear:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Too few parameters: a different input with the same gradient.} With $r = \ell = 1$
  there are $N$ effective parameters for $N$ unknowns. The best restart reached an exact match on
  every seed, but on a different input in 16 of 20 seeds at 4 qubits and 20 of 20 at 8 qubits.
  Two of the 16 at 4 qubits lay within 0.14~rad of the truth (``close'' in
  Table~\ref{tab:rq1}).
  Another restart did find the true input on 10 and 7 of those seeds, but it matched no better
  than the wrong one. The gradient does not determine the input here, so the server cannot tell
  which preimage is the client's.
  \item \textbf{One encoding layer, more trainable layers: recovered.} Every $1\times\ell$ circuit
  with $\ell\ge 2$ gave up its input on 20 of 20 seeds, at both sizes, from 12 to 120 effective
  parameters.
  \item \textbf{More encoding repetitions: stuck.} At a fixed parameter count, moving layers from the
  trainable block into encoding repetitions raised the number of stuck attacks. At 8 qubits and
  120 effective parameters the input was recovered on 20, 18, 8 and 2 of 20 seeds for $r = 1, 2,
  4, 8$. At 4 qubits and 60 parameters the counts were 20, 19, 19 and 12. For every shape with
  $r\ge2$, more seeds were stuck at 8 qubits than at 4: $4\times1$, for example, was stuck on 4 of
  20 seeds at 4 qubits and 12 of 20 at 8 qubits.
\end{itemize}
No attack with $r\ge2$ ended ambiguous. Every failure there was a local minimum that matched the
gradient worse than the true input.

\subsection{RQ2: Shot Noise}\label{sec:rq2}
We repeated the three circuits with $r\ell = 4$ ($1\times4$, $2\times2$, $4\times1$) at 4 and 8
qubits, with 28 and 56 effective parameters. The client's gradient was estimated from $S = 10^2$ to
$10^6$ shots per expectation value, for 600 attacks in all (Table~\ref{tab:rq2}, Fig.~\ref{fig:shots}).

per expectation value.}

Qubits & $r\times\ell$ & $10^2$ & $10^3$ & $10^4$ & $10^5$ & $10^6$ \\

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/shot-noise.pdf}
\caption{Median reconstruction error over 20 seeds against shots per expectation value. The dashed
line is 0.2~rad.}
\label{fig:shots}
\end{figure}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{At 4 qubits, shot noise did not stop the attack.} Even at 100 shots the median error
  was 0.137--0.192~rad, with 10--17 of 20 seeds within 0.2~rad. Each tenfold increase in shots
  cut the error by a factor of about 3, close to the $S^{-1/2}$ of the shot noise itself.
  \item \textbf{At 8 qubits, 100 shots protected every circuit}, with median errors of 1.0--2.4~rad
  and at most 1 seed of 20 within 0.2~rad. At $10^4$ shots the $1\times4$ circuit was back to 20
  of 20 seeds within 0.2~rad.
  \item \textbf{Shot noise did not help the attack past local minima.} The 8-qubit $4\times1$ circuit was
  stuck on 11--12 of 20 seeds from $10^4$ to $10^6$ shots, the same as its 12 with exact
  gradients.
  \item \textbf{Noise did not change which seeds got stuck.} The $4\times1$ circuit
  at 4 qubits was stuck on the same 4 seeds with exact gradients and at every shot count from
  $10^2$ to $10^6$, from the same starting points. Those failures come from the loss landscape, not
  from the noise.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Attacker Budget}\label{sec:budget}
A stuck attack only shows that 10 restarts were not enough. We reran the four 8-qubit circuits with
the most stuck seeds using 50 restarts (Table~\ref{tab:budget}). The seeds generate the same input,
parameters and starting points, so the first 10 restarts of each run repeat the RQ1 attack, and
they reproduce its counts exactly.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Restart budget at 8 qubits: seeds recovered (of 20) by the lowest-loss restart among the
first 10 and the first 50, and the fraction of all 1000 restarts that found the input.}
\label{tab:budget}
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{}cccccc@{}}
\toprule
Qubits & $r\times\ell$ & Params & 10 restarts & 50 restarts & Per restart \\
\midrule
\inputrows{tables/budget.tex}
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Most stuck seeds were recovered with more restarts.} Recovered seeds rose from 7 to
  18 ($2\times1$), 8 to 17 ($4\times1$) and 8 to 18 ($4\times2$). Every recovered input matched to
  the precision of the optimizer.
  \item \textbf{$8\times1$ stayed hard}, at 5 of 20 seeds, with 1.1\% of restarts succeeding. At
  that rate an attacker needs about 90 restarts per success on average, against about 13 for
  $2\times1$ (7.9\%).
  \item Encoding repetitions therefore lower the per-restart success rate. A restart took a median
  of 0.87~s on a shared CPU, so 90 restarts cost the attacker under two minutes.
\end{itemize}

\section{Discussion and Limitations}
\emph{What the regimes say about each claim.} Encoding repetitions made the attack harder at a fixed
parameter count, which points the same way as Kumar et al.'s mechanism~\cite{kumar2023}: more
encoding frequencies, more spurious minima. Our encoding raises the frequencies linearly in $r$
rather than exponentially, and our attacker is stronger (exact second-order gradients and
L-BFGS-B instead of 60 ADAM steps), so the setups differ in both directions. The $1\times\ell$
results agree with Papadopoulos et al.~\cite{papadopoulos2025}: once the trainable block gives more
gradient equations than unknowns, the attack succeeded on every seed. With exactly as many
equations as unknowns ($r = \ell = 1$) the gradient had several exact preimages, so even a perfect
optimizer could not identify the input.

\emph{Stuck is not private.} A stuck attack failed with this budget, from these starting points. It
does not show that the input is safe. With five times the restarts, most stuck seeds gave up their
input (Section~\ref{sec:budget}). On these circuits, encoding repetitions behave like a work factor
for the attacker. Kumar et al.\ predict local minima that grow exponentially in their encoding
parameter~\cite{kumar2023}. If that holds for re-uploading too, the work factor would grow with
circuit size, and our two sizes cannot test that.

\emph{Limitations.}
\begin{itemize}
  \item All circuits are simulated and at most 8 qubits. The results show where each claim holds
  at this size, not how it scales.
  \item The client's parameters are untrained and the batch size is 1. Training changes the
  gradient's frequency content: Kumar et al.\ found that fitting a low-frequency target reduced
  privacy~\cite{kumar2023}. Batches mix several inputs into one gradient.
  \item The label is known to the attacker.
  \item Shot noise is the only device noise modelled. Gate and readout noise are future work.
  \item We do not measure trainability, which Heredge et al.\ tie to the same structure that
  enables the attack~\cite{heredge2025}.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}
On simulated 4- and 8-qubit re-uploading circuits, against an attacker who knows the circuit and the
label, we asked when the client's input stays private on most seeds.

With exact gradients, two settings kept the input private on most seeds. With exactly as many
effective parameters as inputs, the gradient had several exact preimages. Against the 8-qubit
$8\times1$ circuit the attack found the input on 1.1\% of restarts, and the input stayed private on
15 of 20 seeds after 50 restarts. Every other circuit leaked its input on most seeds within 10 restarts, or within 50 for
the other three circuits we retested. Moving parameters into encoding repetitions made each restart
less likely to succeed.

Under shot noise we ran 10 restarts and counted a reconstruction within 0.2~rad as a leak. At 8
qubits, 100 shots per expectation value kept every circuit private on most seeds, and 1000 shots did
so for $1\times4$ and $4\times1$. The 8-qubit $4\times1$ circuit stayed private on most seeds at
every shot count, but without noise 50 restarts recovered it on 17 of 20 seeds; we did not run 50
restarts under noise. At 4 qubits every circuit leaked on at least half the seeds at every
shot count we tried.

Whether a client can still train on gradients as noisy as 100 shots, and whether the attacker's cost
grows exponentially with circuit size as Kumar et al.\ predict, are the questions this setup leaves
open.
